title: What is known about 1RB1LD_0RC0RF_1LC0LA_0LE1LD_1LA---_0RB0LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LD_0RC0RF_1LC0LA_0LE1LD_1LA---_0RB0LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is always a handful of blocks of 1s separated by short runs of 0s. One elementary move is proved in Lean (a 0 travelling through a block). The way block lengths change from sweep to sweep looks chaotic: blocks merge, and large blocks are cut in a ratio close to 1:2. No rule on the lengths is known, so nothing is known about halting (E reading a 1).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,722 cells have been visited and 4,713 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.353). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.287).

claims.title: Travelling 0
claims.text: 0 C> 1^n becomes 1^n 0 C> in 3n steps, for every n and any tape around.

claims.title: Block picture
claims.text: In 3·109 steps, every time C stands at the right end the tape is 2 to 8 blocks of 1s separated by 0^2, 0^3 or 0^5, with 0 1 0 C>0 at the end. The last block is close to twice the one before it in most samples (347, 700; 1,113, 2,230; 730, 1,468).

claims.title: Travelling 0
claims.text: 0 C> 1^n becomes 1^n 0 C> in 3n steps, for every n and any tape around.

claims.title: Block picture
claims.text: In 3·109 steps, every time C stands at the right end the tape is 2 to 8 blocks of 1s separated by 0^2, 0^3 or 0^5, with 0 1 0 C>0 at the end. The last block is close to twice the one before it in most samples (347, 700; 1,113, 2,230; 730, 1,468).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts only when E reads a 1. The block lengths change chaotically, and no invariant that keeps E away from a 1 has been found. CTL (windows of 2 to 5 cells) and NGramCPS (widths 2 to 8, with history) fail.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: A 0 travelling right through a block of 1s (c_shift).
No halt in the C simulator; 4,722 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A few blocks of 1s
html:
When state C stands at the right end, the tape is a short list of blocks of 1s (lengths below, separated by 0s):

step  12,164,477   1^2 0^2 1^13 0^2 1^1009 0 1 C>0
step  12,902,116   1^347 0^2 1^700 0 1 C>0
step  13,724,275   1^14 0^2 1^345 0^5 1^693 0 1 C>0
step  14,048,610   1^14 0^2 1^345 0^2 1^231 0^2 1^464 0 1 C>0

In between, sweeps move single 0s through the blocks. A 0 next to C travels right through a block of 1s, three steps per cell (0 C> 1^n → 1^n 0 C>, proved in Lean). This moves one unit from one block to its neighbour per step of three. Blocks touching across a single 0 merge (for example 126 and 40 become 168 at step 150,135).

sections.heading: Splitting by thirds
html: Large blocks are cut up in a ratio close to 1:2. At step 12,174,442 the tape is essentially one block of 1,041; at step 12,902,116 it is 347 and 700. The next sweeps cut the 700 again (345, 231, 464). This splitting by thirds is reminiscent of Collatz-like maps. Here, though, several blocks interact, and the lengths do not follow any rule found so far. The total number of 1s grows slowly (6,891 after 3·109 steps), the left side grows like the square root of the step count and the right side like a smaller power.

What halting would need. The machine stops when E reads a 1. E is entered from D on a 0 (writing 0, moving left). A halt would need some block arrangement that sends D left onto a 1 where it usually finds a 0. Ruling that out needs a description of the block dynamics, which is not known yet.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.353). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.287).
After 109 steps the tape spans 4,722 cells (3,638 left of the start, 197 right), with a density of 1s of 0.998.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

summary: An abacus of a few blocks of 1s: sweeps move units between neighbouring blocks, blocks merge, and a big block is split into about a third and two thirds; the block lengths evolve chaotically.
